query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled, optimized thermal/thermomechanical treatment that induces the formation of nanoscale, coherent precipitates along the grain boundaries will enhance the load-bearing integrity and crack resistance of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy while preserving its field- and pressure-induced caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: The as-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits coarse grain boundaries with inhomogeneities that lead to poor load-bearing integrity and cracking, even though it maintains a large caloric effect in field- and pressure-driven refrigeration cycles.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored thermal/thermomechanical treatment with processing parameters (temperature kept below the transformation-critical threshold, controlled hold time, and cooling rate) that promotes the precipitation of a minute, coherent secondary phase along grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: The treatment should occur at a temperature sufficiently high to activate nucleation and growth of nanoscale precipitates but remain below the temperature at which the bulk phase transformation kinetics (critical for caloric performance) are affected. Post-treatment evaluations should be conducted under refrigeration operating temperatures and under applied-field (magnetic/electric) as well as pressure conditions, with mechanical loading in the regime where cracking was observed previously.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent precipitates distributed along grain boundaries resulting in a refined intergranular architecture.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates act as crack deflection and pinning sites that bolster the grain boundaries to improve toughness and crack resistance. By carefully controlling the thermal exposure, the grain interior, which drives the reversible phase transformations responsible for the caloric response, remains largely unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to show significantly improved load-bearing capacity and crack resistance (e.g., at least a 20% improvement in fracture toughness) while maintaining essentially the same magnitude of field- and pressure-induced caloric response (no more than a 10% change in caloric parameters) compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits excellent caloric performance under applied-field and pressure-field conditions but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and a tendency to crack under operational loads.
generation.boundary: Processing temperatures must not exceed the threshold that would alter the active phase transformation kinetics engaged during refrigeration operation; mechanical testing should remain within the operational temperature and stress regimes relevant to the application.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise processing parameters (temperature, time, cooling rate) needed to optimize precipitate size and distribution without perturbing the caloric phase transformations. Fine-tuning these parameters may require iterative testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples. The experimental set will undergo the tailored thermal/thermomechanical treatment while the control set will remain untreated. Subject both sets to mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness, hardness, and bending tests) and measure their caloric response (e.g., adiabatic temperature change or entropy change) under typical applied-field and pressure-field conditions within the refrigeration operating temperature range.
measurements: Fracture toughness and crack propagation resistance
Yield strength and hardness under relevant mechanical loads
Caloric effect parameters (entropy change or adiabatic temperature change) under applied-field and pressure conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit at least a 20% improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., decreased crack propagation and enhanced fracture toughness) or if the caloric response is degraded by more than 10% relative to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

At this temperature, while the primary solid HEB phase is maintained, at the interface, HEB and boron carbide form a eutectic liquid that can penetrate and fill the voids between the grains and lead to the formation of a low–melting point intergranular Zr-rich dodecaboride (ZrB12) phase. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) revealed that the boron carbide phase can form coherent structures with the HEB, suggesting that the HEB grain surface provides nucleation sites and guides the grain growth for the boron carbide during the cooling process. frame.system: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy in its as‐developed/operational state. It is a multifunctional refrigeration material that shows a large caloric (field‐ and pressure-induced) response but suffers from low load‐bearing integrity and cracking.
frame.goal: Increase the alloy’s mechanical integrity (i.e., load-bearing capacity and crack resistance) without degrading its favourable caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field conditions used in refrigeration.
frame.limitation: Poor load-bearing integrity and a propensity to crack, which undermine the material's reliability during mechanical loading and cyclic field operations.
constraints: Only a single intervention can be applied
The intervention must not diminish the caloric response
Intervention must be effective under both applied-field (e.g., magnetic/electric) and pressure-field operating regimes
frame.regime: The material is intended to operate under refrigeration conditions with applied fields (magnetic, electric) and cycling pressure. This implies that the intervention must be stable across temperature ranges relevant to the caloric effect and mechanical load boundaries encountered during field cycling.
prior_attempts: While not detailed explicitly in the question, previous strategies in similar high-entropy alloys have involved compositional tweaks or processing routes that improved mechanical properties but often at the expense of the caloric effect.
frame.understanding: A plausible mechanism is that a small microalloying or processing intervention could refine the microstructure (for example, by introducing grain-boundary strengthening precipitates or ductility-enhancing phases) which enhances toughness and load-bearing capability. The fine precipitates or modified grain boundary chemistry should ideally pin cracks and inhibit propagation without interfering with the martensitic or other caloric phase transformations that underlie the caloric response.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on related multi‐component alloys have increasingly focused on engineering the microstructure to enhance mechanical integrity. For example, one line of work (PMC5321736) demonstrated that promoting a 3D twin network can enhance strength, ductility, and toughness by creating effective crack‐stopping features, while another (PMC6841954) showed that in‐situ formation of fine, reinforcing particles (such as SiC) via compositional modification can substantially boost hardness and tensile strength. The progression has been from relying on deformation‐induced twin architectures to deliberately introducing secondary phases to bolster load‐bearing capacity. However, these interventions in “conventional” high‐entropy alloys have sometimes altered the active transformation pathways or compromised functional properties, indicating that the key challenge remains to enhance mechanical properties without interfering with the underlying caloric (phase transformation) response.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved issue is to formulate a single-step intervention that strengthens the alloy’s microstructure (improving load-bearing integrity and crack resistance) while preserving the reversible phase transformation mechanisms that are critical for its large caloric response. Prior approaches using compositional changes or processing modifications have improved mechanical performance, but they risk altering the transformation kinetics that underpin the caloric effect.
decision.lever: Introduce a controlled, optimized thermal/thermomechanical treatment to engineer a refined grain boundary architecture with dispersion of nanoscale, coherent precipitates (or stabilization of favorable twin boundaries) along the intergranular regions.
decision.why: This approach logically extends prior trends: by focusing on microstructure architecture rather than bulk composition modification, it is possible to enhance crack resistance and load-bearing integrity via grain boundary strengthening without disturbing the active, field-driven phase transformations that yield the caloric effect. The treatment would be optimized (in terms of temperature, time and cooling rate) to precipitate a minute volume fraction of a secondary phase at grain boundaries that acts to pin and blunt cracks, as seen in analogues from previous high-entropy alloy studies, while keeping the matrix largely unaffected so that the caloric response under applied-field and pressure conditions is preserved.
